thesis: History shows that every major form of taxation was originally sold as temporary crisis management, then quietly calcified into permanent infrastructure—because the state always finds it easier to keep collecting than to stop.
hook: In 991 CE, a terrified English king paid ten thousand pounds of silver to Viking raiders to make them go away. He called it Danegeld. It was never paid again. Just kidding—it's still being paid. We just renamed it.
stakes: This isn't ancient history. Every tax you pay today was once a temporary measure. The income tax was 1913. The wartime excess profits tax of 1917. The telephone tax. The airport tax. They're all still here, and they all started as emergencies that were supposed to end.
counterpoint: Some will argue that governments need reliable revenue to function, and that consistency requires permanence. But the Danegeld was born of the exact same logic—once you start collecting, the infrastructure wants to survive.
implication: You're not paying taxes because they're permanent. You're paying taxes because the collection infrastructure outlived the crisis that created it. The receipts never lie—the state never gives the money back.
close: That Saqqara tomb painting—scribes tallying grain while farmers watch with expressions unchanged in five thousand years—tells you everything. The method evolved. The relationship didn't. And the collection never stopped. So next time someone says your taxes are the price of civilization, ask them which crisis they're still paying for.
